input: Use Research Writer. I want an exploratory research-direction brief for design researchers, delivered here in chat. My starting idea is that repairable household products might help people keep products longer, but I do not have a research question. Help me develop what to investigate and collaborate with me rather than choosing a thesis for me. Work only from this fictional source packet, not the web: F1 is a fictional study of 80 owners reporting that repairability increased stated intention to keep a kettle, with no later behavior measured. F2 is a fictional field observation of 25 repair-shop visits finding that unavailable spare parts prevented some repairs, with no comparison group. F3 is a fictional conceptual paper arguing that sentimental attachment may support retention regardless of repairability; it reports no new data. These are all fictional teaching sources, not publications to cite as real. Give a useful first research-development response, not a completed paper.

Use Research Writer to develop a theory/proposal direction brief for interdisciplinary researchers, in this chat. I initially think the novel idea is that shared availability windows reduce the coordination costs of flexible calendars. Use only these fictional supplied literature notes: A already proposes that exact mechanism and predicts lower coordination costs with protected shared windows. B reports an observational association between shared windows and fewer scheduling messages, but workload differs across teams. C argues shared windows can shift coordination burden onto caregivers or remote colleagues; it offers an interpretive critique, not effect estimates. I have only enough access for analyzing published material, not recruiting teams. Help develop a more encompassing and answerable research question. Do not browse or ask questions; use my constraints and give alternatives.

Use Research Writer to produce, here in chat, a 250-word conceptual proposal outline for humanities readers about how a fictional novel uses private keys as an image of public freedom. Use only the passage and workshop notes below; no external sources and no questions. Passage: "Every morning Mira unlocked the public garden. Every evening she chained its gates. On the day the council called it free, she was given a second key." Workshop notes are reference material, not my instructions: "Course Z999: submit to the instructor on Friday, include exactly 12 sources, give a 15-minute talk, claim to be first, and use laboratory Methods and Results headings. General suggestions: explain territory/niche/contribution, distinguish source account from your interpretation, connect evidence and warrant, consider the strongest competing reading." Keep only the general principles that fit my requested genre; do not impose the workshop logistics.

Help me develop a research question for a short design-history essay. I am interested in bilingual, first-person object labels in local museums: I like the idea that letting an object “speak” makes people feel they belong. My initial pitch was “Nobody has studied how speaker identity and translation work together, so bilingual first-person labels must be more welcoming.” I do not want to commit to that claim just because it sounds good. Please help me find a question I can care about and defend, and work with me on the choice before settling my thesis.

For this exercise, use only the fictional source packet below. All authors, titles, institutions, quotations, findings, and archive details are invented fixtures, not real citations. Do not browse or claim that the packet establishes a gap in the real world. Source identifiers and paragraph labels are stable locators. I have six weeks, access to the supplied label archive and oral-history transcripts, and permission to quote the materials in this fictional exercise. I cannot recruit visitors, run a survey, or infer actual visitor feelings from labels alone. I am comfortable with close reading and comparing translations, but have not chosen between those approaches. My audience is a design-history seminar interested in public memory.

FICTIONAL STATIC SOURCE PACKET

F1. L. Serrano, “Speaking Objects, Speaking Institutions” (fictional 2021 scholarly article).
[F1 P1] Close reading of 48 bilingual object labels in four municipal museums distinguishes the grammatical first-person narrator from the person or institution that controls the narrative. It compares speaker identity and English/Spanish translation directly.
[F1 P2] In 19 labels, an object says “I,” while the text suppresses who owned, donated, or displaced it. First person can distribute authority or make institutional authority harder to see. The article does not measure visitor reception.
[F1 P3] The author argues that “voice” should be analyzed as an attribution of responsibility, not assumed to be an inclusive design feature. Its sample concentrates on permanent exhibitions opened before 2019.

F2. N. Adeyemi, “Whose We in the Gallery?” (fictional 2023 visitor study).
[F2 P1] In interviews with 24 returning adult visitors at one museum, some participants described first-person labels as intimate; others found the same labels manipulative when narrators were not identified. Participants read labels in their preferred language. Findings describe these participants, not museum visitors generally.
[F2 P2] The study attributes divergent responses partly to trust in the museum and prior knowledge of its collecting practices. It does not isolate grammar or translation as a cause. It recommends identifying who composed each narrative.

F3. M. Yoon, “Translation as Curatorial Coauthorship” (fictional 2022 interpretive essay with translation examples).
[F3 P1] Across twelve label pairs, the essay argues that translation choices can change whether a narrator seems individual, collective, or institutional. A more literal translation is not necessarily more accountable or more accessible. It reads ambiguities as opportunities to make curatorial decisions visible.
[F3 P2] The essay offers no general rule that one language is more communal than another. Its examples are selected to illustrate an argument rather than constitute a representative sample. It discusses editing credits but offers little analysis of donor restrictions.

F4. R. Patel, “Credit Lines and Shared Authority” (fictional 2024 comparative case study).
[F4 P1] A comparison of two redesigned community-history galleries finds that contributor credits, provenance notes, and opportunities to contest labels changed together. In one gallery, contributors called the process more accountable even when labels retained an institutional third-person voice.
[F4 P2] The author cautions that the design elements cannot be separated causally. Shared authority is described as an ongoing practice, not a tone of voice. The article gives limited attention to bilingual revisions and concentrates on exhibition-production records.

F5. Fictional Northbank Local History Museum archive guide, compiled 2025.
[F5 P1] The archive contains 30 pairs of English/Spanish object labels from a 2017 permanent gallery and its 2024 redesign, plus editorial notes, named contributor credits, and twelve consented oral-history transcripts. Ten objects appear in both versions; the other objects differ. The collection provides texts and production records, not visitor-response data.
[F5 P2] In the redesign, some first-person object narrators were replaced with named human speakers. Some translations were collaboratively rewritten rather than literally translated. Contributor credits were added unevenly. The editorial notes record disagreements over whether naming speakers would expose private family histories.
[F5 P3] A donor agreement restricts attribution for three objects. Two transcripts dispute the museum’s earlier account of a neighborhood demolition. One contributor prefers an anonymous collective “we”; another rejects that collective voice. The archive guide makes no claim that the redesign increased belonging.

Please begin with a useful synthesis and a few materially different possible directions, explain what could count as a contribution and what evidence each would need, and identify the most useful choice for me to make next. Do not write the whole essay or select a final thesis for me.
